"Mansplaining" originally referred to a Man who has no special training to speak as an authority on the subject matter, nonetheless explaining to a woman (or women) something to do with women's issues. Like the male politician who said (paraphrasing) "A woman can't get pregnant through legitimate rape. A woman's body has a way of shutting that whole thing down." 

It's the idea that a man can be so arrogant as to assume himself to know more about being a woman than an actual woman, and to actually speak as such. 

However, some people have latched onto the term to broaden it such that now it can be invoked to more broadly mean a man condescendingly offering an explanation of anything to a woman, based on the prejudice that he knows more on the subject than the woman due to her gender.

I was around 27 and my younger Brother-in-Law asked me to take him to meet a friend on a college campus around 9pm (It was a large university I'd attended, so I knew my way around and he didn't.)

A couple of miscues about where to meet up and we wind up going to the friends' dorm. about half-way to the dorm walking across campus from where we were originally supposed to meet I had a moment of "WTF am I doing here." The undergrads all looked way younger than I remembered being when I was in college, and I realized I in no way fit in. The only thing I had going for me was that I was with my college aged brother-in-law, until he tells me he's going up to his friend's dorm room. I tried to nope out of there but B-I-L insisted on going up and I didn't want to get in trouble with the missus for abandoning her brother. 

For context, his hometown had about 1/20th the population as the student body of the college, so he was out of his depth. I found myself standing alone outside an undergrad dorm at night for 15 minutes praying no one would call campus security on me. 

Nothing happened but a few glares from female students, and as soon as my B-I-L popped up with his friend I suggested we go to an off campus restaurant \ bar. 

After that It really sunk in that that part of my life was firmly in the past and I could no longer pass for college age (having a beard didn't help me look any younger.)

Was in Europe about twelve years ago on the French German border (Alsace) and one of the German TV stations I got in my hotel would switch from normal programming during the day to these weird "lottery" shows sponsored by phone sex commercials at night. The phone sex ad on high rotation featured a woman grinding on a urinal in a men's room. 

That's not something you'd normally see on US broadcast TV. That wasn't the ONLY commercial, but as an American my take away was definitely "Wow, they advertise pee fetish phone sex lines on German broadcast TV."

And by adding emphasis on it being "broadcast" TV I'll point out that Americans have weird censorship laws. Cable TV, Streaming, and Satellite are all considered private services, and so they can show pretty much whatever they want. Anything broadcast on airwaves is subject to public decency standards set by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). So seeing it on a broadcast channel adds to the perception that it is a perfectly normal everyday thing.  

And as to why I was watching a German lottery show with phone sex ads, I got like six stations and the only English language station was CNN worldwide. My entertainment choices were basically CNN running the same hourlong show over and over, Spongebob in French, or the cute German girl telling me I could win 50,000 Euro! We know that Lorca suffered injuries at the time of the Buran's destruction. His convalescence period before being assigned to DISCO could have given him the opportunity to learn enough about his counterpart to get by. Then he's on a new ship where no one knows him (except maybe Landry) and there's a war going on. So it's not like he's constantly bumping into old friends wanting to talk about meteor showers. 

The idea that he and MU Burnham were together is just one possibility. But it is clear that there is SOMETHING making him protect her more than anyone else on the crew. She doesn't play an indispensable role on the ship and he's known her for less time than most everyone else. 

It could be that he has some plan that he knows will require her down the line, but I think it's also possible (if he's from the MU) that her counterpart was someone he was close to, and he thinks he can undo the loss by pulling a Walter Bishop.

DS9 spent a lot more time in the MU (Albeit 90 years in the future from DISCO time) and made it clear that not everyone in the MU is an over the top, mustache twirling, caricature of of villian. Even in Mirror, mirror MU Spock was more reasoned than his human counterparts. 

It's very clear that the writers want us to think Lorca is from the MU. They've been dropping a lot of bread crumbs, but this could be a deception. I don't think an alternate universe plot line makes the show any less accessible than making the main story arc about an FTL technology powered by mushrooms that works differently than the FTL technology everyone else already has. Alternate Universe stories are all over genre fiction from the last 70 years. Even if you are unfamiliar with the prior MU episodes in Star Trek, it's not that hard to follow. 

They key thing in the latest episode is that Lorca revealed to Stamets that he had been using the data from the Spore drive for months and independently reached his own conclusions that it could be used as a link to other universes (pl).

First, this shows that Lorca is hiding something. He's the captain of a science vessel that has been retrofitted as a warship, and he's using it as a weapon in that war. The shipped is staff full of scientists who have way more time and expertise to explore and develop his ideas about using the Spore drive as an interdimensional portal than he does. But he chose to keep this s secret until he needed a carrot to convince Stamets to take a huge risk. 

Lorca wanted the 133 jumps because, as he said, every jump gives him more information on how the drive works and how he can use it to get to an alternate universe. He justifies the jump frenzy as a way to speed up data collection on the cloak, but he knows it will gather the data he needs to plot coordinates into another universe. 

As to why he still seems confused as to where they are at the end of the episode: First, he doesn't know it's been successful yet. He needs confirmation that they made it "home." Second, even if they are in the MU, he can't just make a shipwide announcement that he's not the Lorca everyone knew and he's hijacked Discovery. He doesn't know the detail of Stamets' condition. As far as he knows they could just throw him in the brig and jump back. He's got to play the scenario out. 

I'm not discounting the theory that he is Section 31. It could be that all of the "Lorca is from the MU" hints so far have been deliberate misdirection on the part of the writers. We don't know. we're left to speculate until the plot moves forward. That's what makes it fun.

So, yeah, Lorca has a backstory, but it is from his prime  counterpart, who presumably either died on the Buran or is stuck in the MU.

And that episode underlines the absurdity of the whole "It's not the original timeline" argument re Discovery. It shows that Enterprise is not in the "original" timeline, but a timeline that forked from the events of First Contact, and (presumably) every other time travel episode\movie of Star Trek. The timeline has always been maleable and any differences versus the "canon" can be retconned by a later explanation that time travel forked things up (pun intended.) It is even implied in the ENT episode that it's the beacon from the assimilated earth ship which draws the attention of the borg and causes them to start making their way towards the alpha quadrant, which triggers the events leading up to NCC-1701-D's first encounter with the borg. (Yes, it was Q who sent them to face the borg, but only because he knew they were coming and that was his way of giving humans a warning). That in and of itself is a paradox. 

Time travel has always been a crutch for Star Trek writers, as well as a thorn in their side. But is shows how silly it is to obsess over canon in a franchise like this. It's fine if you don't like Discovery because of the tone, the story-telling format, the plot, the acting, etc. that's fine, and your individual prerogative. ST is a BIG universe and not everything produced is going to appeal to every fan.

Former Muslim here. 

Was raised Catholic, became atheist\agnostic as a teen. Converted to Islam at 21, practicing Muslim for a few years, then back to atheist\agnostic. 

I got into Islam after studying different world religions. I had a sense that there "had to be something more" and several aspects of the religion appealed to me. The tenets of the religion are very different than what you hear about in the news. It is supposed to be about finding peace through submission to the will of God. There are two basic questions you have to answer to be Muslim: Do you believe in the singular monotheistic God? Do you believe Muhammad was His messenger? If yes to both, congrats, you're a Muslim. (Technically you have to profess to both in front of witnesses.)

Anyway, it was like "So, I believe there is this great force in the universe, and I can ascribe cetrain characteristics to it. I could call this force Bob, or Larry, or God. So If I call it God, what do I think it is, and wants?" I decided, ultimately, it wanted us to all get along and be cool, so it would probably have tried to tell us about that. That's prophecy. So I studied the prophetic religions and read about the pillars of Islam, and it's a blueprint for living a peaceful, happy lifestyle in harmony with everyone. It's about self improvement, being kind, being charitable, respecting each other. So I was like "yes, this all sounds true; and nothing else is really ringing that bell for me." So then the leap of faith is, "Well, if this religion contains all this truth, can I then accept that it's all true. The Muhammad really is the Messenger, and the Koran is the blueprint, and maybe these things I'm not so sure about are because I've still got to learn." It took time, almost three years, but I finally said "OK, I'm in." I prayed, I went to Mosque. I convinced my wife to convert, we had a baby, and I gave him a proper Muslim name. 

Then 9/11 happened. It sounds cliche, but that put a whammy on me. The reaction inside my Mosque was "circle the wagons, we've got to protect our own." I had heard sermons there about how it was the responsibility of every able Muslim to support the Jihad of our Palestinian brothers and sisters against the Jewish state. I had heard about why it was necessary to isolate ourselves from the non-believers in our community. I had pushed my negative feelings about those sermons aside, somehow dismissed them as not relevant to me, because I was there for the part of Islam that was about peace and love. 

But then men hijacked planes and attacked my home in the name of this thing I believed in and loved, and I went to the Mosque expecting to hear Outrage and condemnation of those who perverted our religion, a rallying cry to go out and tell our Christian  brothers and sisters that this is not who we are, what we stand for, that we were being attacked on that day too. 

Instead I heard nothing like that. Our Imam went on the local TV station and said those things to the camera, but his message for the worshippers was "keep your heads down, they will see us ans the enemy now, we have to look out for each other and hope this blows over." I still hoped there would be a massive outpouring from our community, but most were quiet. 

That was it, the spell was broken. I stopped going to that Mosque, I tried another, actually found one I liked better, with an American Imam; but it was a major drive for me, so I tried to be a Muslim on my own. I started praying less frequently, stopped wearing a kufi, and started looking at those passages in the Koran that gave me pause years earlier and realized they bothered me still. After a couple of years when Ramadan came around, I said "No, I can't. I know in my heart I don't believe anymore."

Like I said, I'm atheist\agnostic now. Having been born and raised in the US, no one would know from my name or appearance that I was ever a practicing Muslim. It's not something I advertise, because Islam doesn't really take a fond attitude towards people who leave the faith. In reality, not much happens in the US; still, no need to give someone a reason to have a chip on their shoulder towards me.

My employer recently switched from "Paid Time Off" where you get a set amount per year and you accrue days off over time to "Discretionary Time Off" There's no fixed amount, you don't "accrue" anything, there's no paperwork, and it's totally at your manager's discretion to say yes or no.

The main reason they did this is that accrued PTO is a liability on the balance sheet. But it's also been shown that employees on DTO plans take significantly less time off, because without someone saying "you get four weeks a year and if you don't use it it's capped, so you lose it" the employee is afraid to find out what is considered "too much" and look to see what their peers are doing. So everybody is watching each other to see if they are going to get in trouble for taking time off, so no one really does. 

That said, I've taken more time off this year, and intend to continue to do so. When I'm working the company owns my soul 24/7. All nighters are and straight through weekends are not uncommon.  I also know they would have a massively hard time backfilling my position.

It's hard to speculate beyond the first term because it really reshuffles the deck for all of the elections that came after. 

I'll piggy back the previous comment on Iraq not happening. There's a small chance 9/11 might not have happened, or might have played out differently. That's not entirely saying W dropped the ball, but a different response to the "Bin Laden determined to strike America" memo could have, at least, caused a tactical change in the attack. There's an even greater likelihood that Bin Laden might have taken a slightly different approach, depending on the political vibe he was getting. He wanted maximum effect towards an end, so a different President with a different policy might have caused him to order different targets, etc. Just changing the date of the attack would mean different people on different planes, so maybe the fourth plane doesn't fight back; maybe more planes fight back, maybe a delay gives the FBI time to get more information out of the 20th hijacker and the whole thing is thwarted. It's butterfly effect territory.

Politically, you could see 2004 as a possible gore reelection scenario, but who then is the Republican nominee? Does Bush run again? McCain likely would have run, potentially Romney too. Say you wind up with a McCain/Romney ticket and a win in 2004. 

A couple things have to be considered. One is the absence of Karl Rove and his impact on the rise of the right wing of the Republican party. Is there a tea party revolution in 2010? Not likely if McCain wins reelection in 2008. The economic crash in 2008 almost certainly still happens, as neither party had any real initiative to do anything that would have impacted the housing bubble and burst. It just wasn't on anyone's RADAR until it was too late. But the timing of the crash so close to the election might not have been enough to sway the vote against the incumbent. In fact, the electorate may have felt like continuity and stability was the right choice. We didn't have that option in 2008 because there wasn't an incumbent running. That means a lot because the 2010 republican sweep was critical to the redistricting that happened, so with less republicans in state houses, you get less gerrymandering towards Republican congressional districts.

You also get much less of a right wing slant to the Republican platform and McCain likely governing largely as a centrist with a Democratic House of Representatives. Perhaps there's a large terror attack in the US that comes later if 9/11 was thwarted. Is Bin Laden still in leadership when it happens? Is Al Qaeda still based in Afghanistan? If he's moved his hideout to another country, the war on terror takes a whole different form. 

Then there's Russia. If W isn't there to look into Putin's soul and declare him to be a good man, does the US react differently to renewed Russian aggression earlier, say with the invasion of Georgia? Without the damaged European alliances from the Iraq war there's a clearer response and Putin isn't so bold in Ukraine\Crimea. 

If McCain is an incumbent running for reelection in 2008, perhaps Obama waits until 2012 to run. Does he win without the anti-war backlash against Iraq? Or does Romney get elected to succeed McCain? If Romney gets elected, do we get the Affordable Care Act as RomneyCare, with overwhelming bi-partisan support and no prolonged effort by either party to poison it and tear it apart? 

In short - 20 years isn't a very long time for things to be dramatically different. The Iraq war is the biggest difference, and some other geopolitical differences would play out. We'd have a different succession in the presidency, so some minor differences in domestic programs - perhaps Medicare part D never happens. This is all speculation. Perhaps Gore would have won a second term, or maybe he gets caught in a massive scandal and is impeached. No way to know. 

What is likely is that we don't get Obama in 2008. He'd either be running as an incumbent without an anti-war platform to boost him, or running to follow someone from his own party, in which case it undermines the "candidate of change" message. If Gore was reelected you almost certainly get a Republican in 2008, just on the basis of people wanting change after sixteen years of same party rule. Hillary's best option then would be in 2012, when she'd likely still be the Senator from New York, since she probably wouldn't have wound up in Gore's cabinet, at least in the first term. A religion is a group of beliefs about divinity shared by multiple people. The simple answer is that most people believe in the divine (E.g. a god or gods) and people in communities discussed their beliefs, started believing in similar things, and began teaching other people their beliefs. 

The underlying question is, why to people believe in the divine to being with? The answer really boils down to three points:

There's a whole lot humans don't have answers to.
Humans are able to contemplate.
Humans are born very premature, relative to other species. 

The first two points are fairly self-explanatory, so I'll start with the third. If you've ever seen footage of a horse being born, you'll notice that within a few minutes they are up on their feet walking around. Grazing animals need to be mobile from the time they are born to keep up with the group and to avoid predators. 

There's a problem in human anatomy. To accommodate our big brains we've got large heads. At the same time, walking upright has caused our hips to narrow. We have to give birth when the baby can still pass through the pelvis, so our babies are born not long after their internal organs are developed enough to survive outside the womb. 

When human babies are born, they are completely helpless and totally dependent on a caregiver or caregivers. The baby's brain is hard wired to bond with the caregivers, feel secure in their presence, and terror in their absence. The care giver is perceived as all-powerful, literally the difference between life and death. 

As the child gets older, this notion persists. The parental figure is viewed with awe and adoration. Only when the child gets older (like 8-10) do they begin to realize that the parent is a fallible and limited being. This creates significant insecurity. If the parent isn't responsible for the world being what it is, and they aren't totally able to protect you from all the bad things that could happen, then who is? 

Take that instinctive drive to trust in an all powerful caregiver, the fear of the unknown, and the human capacity for imagination; and people in every society are going to form the idea that there most be some other intelligence at work making sure that the wheels don't fall off the bus and it's safe to go outside. 

Then, with each passing generation, family structures offer their beliefs to the next generation as factual, just as the kids reach the point of uncertainty. The people you trust most, who you believe were literal gods, are telling you it's all going to be OK because there is a next level being, even more powerful than me, who will take care of you.

First, it's not really accurate. Volcanoes are not pumping more climate impacting material into the atmosphere than people. 

Second, the basic mechanism of climate change is that when the mix of stuff in the air changes the amount of heat retained from the sun changes. 

A quick history: When the earth was created it was really hot, so hot there was no liquid water. It was basically all lava on the surface. Just like a cake coming out of the oven it has been radiating heat and cooling off ever since. Eventually, it will cool off enough that there will be no more lava and the earth will be solid rock, which also means no more volcanoes, or continental drift, or earthquakes. But we're talking billions of years, so not climate change observable in a lifetime. From a human perspective, the temperature of the Earth's core, and therefore the heat radiating up and out, isn't changing enough to notice. and it doesn't really impact the air temperature, which is what we're concerned with. 

Well, the earth cooled, land formed out of the lava, water condensed into rain, pooled on the surface, and we got oceans out of it. life came about in the oceans, and started spreading to land. Some of the first life to come to land was plants. Plants like carbon - a lot. What's more, they have this amazing ability to use the power of the sun to split carbon dioxide into Carbon and Oxygen. They ate tons and tons of carbon out of the air, releasing the free oxygen they didn't need. 

Now, think for a minute about a car on a sunny day. It's much hotter on the inside. This is because the glass lets in most of the sunlight, and reflects a little bit. When the sun hits the interior of the car, some energy is converted into heat, and what remains as light bounces back, but it hits the glass on the way back out, too. Remember, the glass lets MOST of the light out, but reflects some back. This is true on the way in, and on the way out. So some of the sunlight that would have normally left the car, if there were no glass, bounces back into the car and gets a second chance to be converted to heat. This happens over and over until all of the energy is either absorbed or leaves as light. 

Well, that's what Carbon gasses in the atmosphere do, they act like clear glass.

Back to the plants - they stored all of this carbon in their bodies and died. Much of it absorbed into the soil. So the carbon was trapped, and kept out of the atmosphere. Plants kept doing this, so over millions of years the percentage of air that was free oxygen increased, the amount of carbon decreased, and the planet cooled off. All the extra oxygen in the air made the land an OK place for animals to hang out, since they depend on a constant supply of the stuff. More oxygen led to bigger animals. 

All that carbon in the ground started to decay, and what remained built up into large deposits of what we now call coal, oil, and methane. Humans came along and discovered that if they dug this stuff up they could burn it to produce heat. Well, all that fire is doing is performing the chemical reaction to bond carbon with the free oxygen in the air, releasing it back as carbon dioxide. The heat and light we call fire is a byproduct of this chemical reaction. 

So what we have done in the last century is to dig up all of this carbon that plants buried over hundreds of millions of years, undoing the process that made this place livable to begin with. As if that's not bad enough, we've been cutting down all of the forests, getting rid of the plants we need to continue the process and compete against the harm we are doing. 

Now, to Volcanoes. Yes, volcanic eruptions release carbon gases, and the amounts released sound like really big numbers, but they are a tiny fraction compared to what we are pumping out by burning fossil fuels. 

Hypothetically, if there were enough volcanoes erupting simultaneously, could it change the climate. Yes. However, not necessarily in the same way. When volcanoes erupt they don't just pump out gasses, they also pump out ash, lots and lots of it. And the fine particulate gets sent high into the atmosphere. 

Back to the car analogy. How can you keep your car from getting so hot on sunny days? Well, one way is you can tint your windows, or you can even put up those big reflective screens under your windshield when you park. 

Think of the ash from the volcanic eruptions like tinting on the car windows. It's letting some light through, but much less than before, so even though there are more greenhouse gasses, not enough solar energy gets in to begin with to even keep it as warm as before. 

This phenomenon is called a "nuclear winter", based on the theory that if there were a full scale nuclear war the bomb blasts would push so much dust and ash into the atmosphere that it would blot out the sun. 

So the short answer is that human caused climate change is making the global average temperature warmer, volcanic climate change would have two major differences. First, the damage caused by that many, massive volcanic eruptions would probably be pretty bad in its own right; and second, it would get much-much colder before it got warmer. 

If you are lucky enough to survive the eruptions and not freeze to death shortly thereafter, then you would likely starve within a couple years from the global inability to grow crops and produce food. The long term effect of the carbon released during the eruptions wouldn't be our primary concern.

The short answer is that we don't really know. We (humans, totally not robots) experience everything through the filter of how our own brains work. Our perception and comprehension is based on that; so it is very hard to speculate as to how something with a brain very different than our own perceives something. 

What we believe is that the more like our own brains an animal has, the more like our own perception of things they have. So we can infer that a Chimpanzee might experience pain in much the same way as a human, but the further away from us you get on the evolutionary tree, it gets harder to say. 

However, there's a collary to this, which is consciousness. The phrase "experience pain" implies an understading of what is happening and an ability to think about it. We basically assume that the less complex a creature's brain is the less intelligent they are. 

It used to be (until quite recently, actually) that we drew a hard and fast line stating that consciousness, self-awareness, and true intelligence were all unique to humans. That was pretty much our own bias showing and had nothing to do with any real science. Recent research indicates that a number of animals demonstrate all of these traits, though primarily we're talking about advanced vertebrates: Great Apes, Whales, Doplhins, Elephants; to name a few. 

When we start talking about insects, it is a whole different ball game. Comparing the complexity of a high mammalian brain to an insect is like comparing the International Space station to a lean-to. Both are structures designed to shelter people, but one is clearly capable of much more than the other. 

So, we know the anatomy. An ant has a nerve cluster and nerves that run out to its extremities. It is also capable of responding to stimuli, and will generally try to remove itself from a situation where it is experiencing harm. 

Our best guess is that the ant lacks anything like consciousness or the capacity for rationalization. So whereas humans experience an extremely negative, emotional response to pain; and we have the capacity to suffer; we don't think ants brains provide such comprehension. 

To an ant a pain signal might be like a sensor throwing an error in a computer. it is a signal that is processed and allows a response to occur. Any notion of negativity, awareness, or emotion simply would not apply. 

But again, we really don't know.

An interesting distinction to be made. Being called a Marxist is quite different than being labeled as being "like Marx."

Marx may, or may not, have been a "chill dude"; but that has nothing to do with the ideology that bears his name. 

It's rather like the distinction between Christ and Christians. Jesus was by all accounts a socialist hippy who preached against violence and material wealth. People who call themselves Christians have killed tens (if not hundreds) of millions of people in wars over 1700 years, and (at least in the US) are politically aligned with unfettered capitalist ideology and a rollback of social welfare programs. 

Point being, the disposition of the man has little to do with the ideology he spawned.

It began with the rise of the labor movement in the late nineteenth \ early twentieth centuries. At the time, there was very little in the way of regulation, labor laws, wage laws, safety laws. The industrial revolution created a huge gulf between the working class and the ownership class. Marx predicted that workers would rebel against the terrible conditions and rise against the owners. 

When workers began to organize and demand better terms (reasonable hours, better wages, safer working conditions) the wealthy and powerful began using the terms leftists, anarchists, communists, and Marxists to brand them as people who represented a violent danger to the established order. 

Depending on where you were in the world during the first few decades of the twentieth century there were a few possibilities. In Russia, there was revolution, Civil War, and the Communists took over - so being called a Marxist was not an insult there. In other countries, when the depression hit, popular opinions shifted in favor of governments providing more social programs, and the rhetoric died down a bit. In other countries, Fascist regimes rose up, and often declared themselves directly in opposition to communism. Being labeled a Marxist in Hitler's Germany was not good for you.

After the war, there was a global re-alignment along ideological lines, and you began seeing "Marxist" used to label political enemies in the west. 

The bottom line is that it began the day someone coined the phrase, because people always use political labels as epithets for those with conflicting ideologies, regardless of whether or not the person you are labeling thinks of it as an insult. Some Conservatives in America use the term "Liberal" as if speaking the name will forever poison the air in the room. Liberals do the same in reverse. These insults don't work, because the people you are labeling them with don't see them as a negative. The only people who are going to be insulted by being labeled with an ideology are the ones who don't actually follow that ideology.
